newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Sagging sales hit Hyundai Motor, Kia's profits.
newsitem.headline: Sagging sales hit Hyundai Motor, Kia's profits.

text.p: The profitability of South Korea's two major carmakers deteriorated in the first half from a year ago, due largely to slumping domestic sales, company officials and analysts said on Thursday.
But analysts said car sales may pick up, albeit slightly, in the second half in line with an expected economic recovery.
"Domestic sales fell more than 10 percent in the first half. But we can cautiously expect a recovery in the latter half," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
"We will probably see a four or five percent decline in domestic sales for the whole of 1997."
However, some analysts said conditions would remain depressed.
"Major companies, except Daewoo Motor, are planning to introduce new models so they must expect more severe competition," said Huh Ghang, Hyundai Securities auto analyst.

South Korea's largest car maker, Hyundai Motor Co, said on Thursday its net profits in the first half had fallen to 28.16 billion won ($31.49 million) from 51.64 billion won a year earlier. Its sales declined to 5.42 trillion won from 5.56 trillion.
"Domestic sales were pretty slow in the first half because of the slowing economy," said a Hyundai spokesman.

Kia Motors Corp, one of the nation's three largest makers, said its losses widened to 37.0 billion won from a 10.34 billion loss a year ago, while its sales rose to 3.39 trillion won from 3.03 trillion.
Kia Motors is the flagship of eighth-ranked Kia Group, which was put under creditors' protection last month.

Analysts said Kia's production and sales would not be affected by its financial problems because the company raked in more than 400 billion won in cash through a 30 percent cash discount sale in July.
They said the debut of three new models by unlisted Daewoo Motor Co since last November also eroded sales of comparable models from Hyundai and Kia.
Daewoo's Lanos compact cars, which began selling late last year, took a big bite out of markets for Hyundai's Accent and Kia's Avella models.
Daewoo launched sales of its bigger Nubira compact cars in February and its Leganza mid-sized sedans in April.
Analysts said Hyundai and Kia had to offer incentives to keep their market share, including non-interest instalment sales, which cut deeply into their profit margins.
Daewoo Motor said its sales in the first half rose to 2.7 trillion won from 2.05 trillion won a year before, but declined to give profit figures.
The company earlier said it hoped to earn 80 billion won in net profits this year on sales of 6.8 trillion won, compared with 23 billion won on 4.35 trillion won sales.
According to figures from the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association, South Korean vehicle makers sold 724,883 vehicles at home in the first half, down from 817,275 units a year earlier.
Analysts said exports were also not good in terms of profitability because car makers forcibly pushed out shipments to compensate for losses in the domestic market.
South Korean carmakers offered at least a five percent discount to dealers in the overseas market to prop up exports, they said.
The auto association said vehicle exports in the first half rose to 638,608 units, up from 572.070 units a year ago. ($1 = 894.30 won)
